entries.narration: Every Scala program in this course travels the same path, and it helps to see it once before writing anything. It starts as a plain text file. That text means nothing to the machine yet. The Scala compiler reads it, parses it into a tree, and checks the type of every expression. If something does not fit, say a piece of text where a number belongs, compilation stops right there. The program never starts, and nothing is printed. When the checks pass, the compiler writes two kinds of output: class files holding bytecode for the Java Virtual Machine, and tasty files holding typed trees that tools and later compilations read. Then the second time begins. The JVM loads the main class, finds the Scala standard library on its classpath, and executes the code, first by interpreting it and then by compiling the busy parts to native code. Only at the very end does our order total appear on the screen. Keeping these two times apart, compile time and run time, is the first debugging skill this course builds.

Before running anything, it is worth knowing which tools are involved, because each one has a version and each version can change what you see. The runner is the scala command, which since Scala three point five is Scala CLI. The compiler is chosen by the project, not by whatever happens to be installed. The JDK is the Java runtime underneath both. The file on the left pins two of these with using directives: the Scala three point three line, and JDK twenty one. A pin like three point three is a line, not a release, so Scala CLI resolves it to a specific patch, and that resolved number is what belongs in your notes. Then two commands report the truth of your machine: scala version, and java dash version. Answer version questions from that evidence, never from memory. One more thing happens on a first run. The runner downloads a compiler, libraries, and sometimes a whole JDK. That is code arriving on your machine, so treat a script from the internet the way you would treat any program: read it before you run it.

Here is the first program, and it already contains the shape of the whole course: an order and its total. The method is marked with the at main annotation, which tells the compiler to generate an entry point, the place where running begins. Inside, the first value is a list of prices. They are written in minor units, so twelve hundred means twelve point zero zero. That choice keeps the arithmetic exact for now; decimals and rounding come later, when they are needed. Notice that no type is written. The compiler infers that prices is a list of integers from the values themselves. The next line asks the list for its sum, which gives an integer, forty two fifty. Then the last line builds a string with interpolation, substituting the total into the text, and prints it. Printing is the only effect here. The println call returns a value of type Unit, which carries no information; it exists to say this was done for its effect. Everything indented under the equals sign is the method's body. Run it, and Total colon four thousand two hundred fifty appears.

There are two ways to run the code from the last section, and they suit different moments. The first is the one you have seen: scala run with the file name. It compiles the whole program, then runs it, and prints the total. The second is the REPL, short for read, evaluate, print, loop. Start it with scala repl, and type the same lines one at a time. Watch what comes back. After the first line, the REPL echoes the name, the inferred type, and the value: prices is a list of integers. After asking for the sum, it prints val res zero colon Int equals four thousand two hundred fifty. The result had no name, so the REPL gave it one, and you can use res zero in the next line. That echo is the real value of the REPL. It answers the question, what type is this, faster than anything else. But a REPL session disappears when you close it. Once an expression does what you want, move it into a file, where it can be run again tomorrow and give the same answer.

The next program decides between two messages, and it is written twice, once on top and once below. Both versions compile to exactly the same program. The top one uses indentation syntax, which this course uses throughout. After an equals sign, or after then, or after else, the lines indented beneath are the block. The condition reads if total is greater than four thousand then, with no parentheses, because the keyword then marks where the condition ends. At the bottom of the method, end order total closes it. End markers are optional; they earn their place on long blocks, where the closing point would otherwise be hard to see. The lower version uses braces. Curly braces open and close each block, and the condition sits in parentheses. This is how Scala two code was written, and plenty of existing code still looks like it, so reading it fluently matters. Nothing about the layout survives into the running program. And when a file needs to move from one style to the other, the compiler's rewrite options can convert it, rather than anyone doing it by hand.

Programs fail, and the fastest way to fix one is to ask first when it failed. The card on the left holds three mistakes, and each one fails at a different stage. The first assigns a piece of text to a value declared as an integer. The compiler rejects it. Nothing runs, and the error names the file, the line, the type it found, and the type it required. Read those two types before anything else. The second compiles without complaint, because asking a list for index five is perfectly well typed. But the list has three items, so at run time it throws an index out of bounds exception. Here the evidence is a stack trace, and the useful line is the first frame that points into your own code. The third is the dangerous one. Tail drops the first price, the sum is thirty fifty, and the program prints it happily. No error, no exception. The only way to catch it is to know the expected answer, forty two fifty, before running. Compile time, run time, logic: name the stage, and you know where to look.

Every value in a Scala program is reached through a name, and the first decision about a name is whether its binding may change. The code on the left makes one of each. Prices is a val, so it is bound once and can never point anywhere else; the commented last line, which tries to reassign it, would be rejected by the compiler. Count is a var, so the line count equals count plus one re-binds it from two to three. Now look at the memory card. The val's arrow to object number one never moved, yet the object itself grew from two prices to three, because plus equals on an array buffer changes the buffer in place. That is the distinction to hold onto. Val makes the name fixed. It says nothing about the object behind it. Immutability of the object comes from choosing an immutable type, which the next chapters lean on heavily. Finally, every name has a scope. A name declared inside a block exists only inside that block, so the same name can be reused elsewhere without collision.

Every expression in Scala has a type, and the compiler works it out before anything runs. Most of the time you do not have to write it. Look at the first line on the left. Three is an integer literal, so quantity is inferred as Int. The next line ends with a capital L, which makes it a Long. Multiply the two, and the compiler widens the Int to a Long first, so subtotal is a Long. That widening is safe; the opposite direction would need an explicit conversion. The label line writes its type out, and that is always allowed. Method parameters are different: they must be annotated, because nothing on the right-hand side could tell the compiler what callers will pass. The last line is the strangest. Sys dot error throws, so it never produces a value. Its type is Nothing, the type at the very bottom, and Nothing fits wherever any type is expected. At the top sits Any, split into AnyVal for numbers and booleans, and AnyRef for objects. That is enough of the hierarchy to read every type in this chapter.

Arithmetic looks like school mathematics until it reaches an edge, and Scala's number types have edges because they have fixed sizes. The first line divides seven by two and gets three, because dividing two integers keeps only the whole part. Make one side a Double, and the answer is three point five. The third line is the one that surprises people. Add one to the largest Int, and the value wraps around to the most negative Int. There is no exception and no warning; the program simply carries on with a wrong number. The fourth line overflows the same way, even though four billion would fit comfortably in a Long, because both operands are Ints and the multiplication happens in Int. The fix is to make an operand a Long before multiplying, as the fifth line does. For money, binary Doubles are the wrong tool, since most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly. BigDecimal can, but rounding then needs a rule you name, like half even. This course stores money as Int cents, and says out loud the range that assumption covers.

Programs spend a lot of time turning values into text, and Scala's interpolators make that direct. An interpolator is a prefix on a string literal. With s, a dollar sign followed by a name, or by an expression in braces, is replaced by that value's text. The first interpolated line on the left uses it to print an order total, splitting cents into whole units and remainder. Run it with a total of four thousand two hundred and five, and it prints forty two point five. That is wrong by a factor of ten in the cents, because the remainder is five, and nothing pads it to two digits. The line below uses f instead. F understands formats such as percent zero three d and percent point two f, and the compiler checks that the value given to each format has a matching type. It prints zero one seven, and forty two point zero five. Raw keeps backslashes exactly as typed, which suits paths. And a triple quoted string keeps its line breaks, with strip margin trimming the indentation up to each bar. Whenever money becomes text, test it with an amount under ten cents.

In many languages, if is a statement: it decides which block runs, and any result has to be stored in a variable declared beforehand. In Scala, if is an expression. It produces a value, so the result can be bound directly. Shipping, on the left, is defined as the value of the whole if. The conditions are tried from the top. The first asks whether the total is at least five thousand, or the customer is a member. Neither holds, so the next condition is checked: at least two thousand. That is true, so the value is three hundred, and the final branch is never evaluated. Notice the double bar. If the left side had been true, the right side would not have been evaluated at all; that is short-circuiting, and it matters when the right side is expensive or could fail. Because every branch gives an Int, shipping is an Int. Remove the final else, and the missing case has no value, so the result is no longer a useful Int. And keep thresholds ordered from most to least specific, or a broad early branch will hide the rest.

Here are two loops that compute the same order total, and the interesting difference is who is in charge of the iteration. The upper loop is a while loop. It owns a counter. It starts the counter at zero, tests it against the length of the list, and steps it by one at the end of each pass. All three are your responsibility. Delete the step, the line i plus equals one, and the test never becomes false, so the loop runs forever. Change the test to less than or equal, and the last pass asks for an index that does not exist, which throws. The lower loop is a for loop over the list itself. It runs once for each price, handing you the element directly. There is no counter, so there is no off-by-one to make. Both loops leave the total at forty two fifty, and both do it the same way: by changing a var. The loop itself returns Unit, and the answer is a side effect. That is fine for now. In chapter five, collection methods compute the same total as a returned value, with no var at all.

A method gives a computation a name, typed parameters, and a result type. The first method on the left computes a line total from a quantity, a price, and a discount. The discount has a default of zero, so the first call, which passes only two arguments, uses it and returns two thousand four hundred. The second call passes its arguments by name, in a different order from the declaration. The compiler matches them by name, so the order no longer matters, and the call reads like a sentence. There is no return keyword in either method. The body is an expression, and its value is the result. The second method is recursive: it calls itself. To sum a list, it adds the first element to the sum of the rest. Each call works on a smaller list, and the base case, an empty list returning zero, is what finally stops it. Without that base case, the recursion would never end. Each pending call holds a stack frame, so a list with a million elements can overflow the stack. The tail rec annotation asks the compiler to prove a method can run as a loop instead.

So far, every value has been a number, a string, or a collection. This section adds one more kind: a value that is itself a computation. The first line on the left is an ordinary method, with tax, which adds twenty percent. The next line binds it to the name add tax, whose type is written with an arrow: Int arrow Int, a function from an integer to an integer. Because a function is expected there, Scala converts the method into a function value automatically. The line below writes a function value directly, as a lambda that halves its input. Now the useful part. Both function values have the same type, so they can sit together in a list. Rules is a list of functions, data that contains behaviour. Mapping over it applies each rule to one thousand, giving twelve hundred and five hundred. The point is not the arithmetic. It is that a new pricing rule can now be added as a new value in a list, without editing a chain of if branches. The rest of this chapter builds on that single idea: computations can be passed around like any other value.

A lambda is a function value written in place, and it always has the same three parts: parameters, an arrow, and a body. The upper card writes one in full. Its type, Int comma Int arrow Int, says it takes two integers and returns one, and the lambda declares both parameters with their types before computing the discounted price. Calling it with two thousand and ten gives eighteen hundred. Most lambdas are not written this way, because the context usually supplies the types. In the lower card, map on a list of integers expects a function from Int to something, so p arrow p times two needs no annotation at all. The next line goes further with the placeholder underscore. Underscore times two means exactly the same thing: the underscore stands for the parameter. Be careful with it, though. Each underscore is a new parameter, so underscore plus underscore takes two arguments, not one argument twice. Use the placeholder for tiny bodies like these filters, and give the parameter a real name as soon as the body grows. And when nothing tells the compiler what is expected, the parameters must carry their types.

A higher-order function is one that takes a function, returns a function, or does both. The code on the left has one of each. Apply all takes a list of prices and a rule, a function from Int to Int, and maps the rule over the list. It knows nothing about discounts. It only knows how to visit each price. Ten off is a rule that removes ten percent, so applying it to twelve hundred and four fifty gives ten eighty and four oh five. At least is different: it is a method that returns a rule. At least five hundred is a function that raises any price below five hundred up to five hundred. Because both are functions from Int to Int, they plug into apply all in exactly the same way. The last line composes them. Ten off and then at least five hundred runs ten off first and feeds its result into the minimum. Starting from four fifty, ten off gives four oh five, and the minimum lifts it to five hundred. Run them the other way round, and the minimum does nothing, then ten percent comes off, giving four fifty. With composition, order is part of the meaning.

A closure is a function value that uses a name from the scope around it, and this section is about exactly what it captures. On the left, rate is a var set to twenty. Add tax is a lambda that computes tax using rate, a name declared outside the lambda. Call add tax with one thousand, and the result is twelve hundred. Now the program sets rate to twenty five and makes the identical call, and the result is twelve fifty. Nothing about the call changed. The memory card shows why. The closure does not hold the number twenty. It holds access to the variable rate itself, and it reads that variable every time it runs. That makes the function's result depend on an input that never appears in its parameter list. A test that passed this morning can fail because some unrelated code changed rate. Capturing a val is safe, because a val can never be re-bound. And the last line shows the general fix: add tax at takes the rate as a parameter. The hidden input has become an explicit one, and every call says exactly what it depends on.

Often one argument is known early, and another only arrives later. A tax rate is set once; prices arrive one at a time. Scala offers three ways to supply arguments in stages, and the cards on the left show them side by side. The first method has two parameter lists: rate in the first, cents in the second. Writing price of twenty supplies only the first list, and what comes back is a function from Int to Int, still waiting for the cents. That is why it can be handed straight to map, which applies it to each price, giving twelve hundred and six hundred. The second card writes the same idea as a curried function value. Its type, Int arrow Int arrow Int, reads as a function that takes a rate and returns a function that takes cents. The third form starts from an ordinary method with two parameters and fixes the rate with an underscore, which marks the parameter still missing. All three end in the same kind of value. Choose parameter lists when one argument genuinely configures the rest, and keep plain calls when nothing is reused.

A pure function is one whose result depends only on its arguments, and which changes nothing else when it runs. The method next on the left is deliberately not pure. Each call adds one to a counter and returns the new count. That makes it a good probe, because with an effect involved, the moment an expression is evaluated becomes visible. The table traces three strategies, each starting from a counter of zero. Twice eager takes an ordinary parameter. Its argument is evaluated once, before the call, so next runs once, and the result is one plus one, two. Twice by name declares its parameter with an arrow before the type. Now the argument is evaluated every time x is used, so next runs twice, and the result is one plus two, three. The lazy val is evaluated once, at first use, and remembered, so the sum is two again. With a pure argument, all three would agree, and only the cost would differ. With an effect, the strategy changes the answer. None of them is asynchronous. The practical rule follows: keep calculations pure, and push effects like printing and mutation to the edges.

Until now, the order has been a list of numbers. This chapter gives it a shape, starting with a class. Order line, on the left, bundles a product code, a quantity, and a unit price with the operations that belong to them. The class's parameter list is its constructor. Two of the parameters are marked val, which makes them public fields: line dot qty reads back two. The unit price has no val. It can be used inside the class, and total uses it, but from outside it is not accessible at all, which is the commented error. Total itself is a def, so it is computed each time it is called, and it can never fall out of step with the fields. The body of the class runs every time an instance is built, which makes it the place for a check. Require tests that the quantity is positive. Build a line with a quantity of zero, and require throws an illegal argument exception carrying your message. That guarantees every order line that exists has a positive quantity. Throwing is a blunt way to say no, though. The next section shows a factory that returns the failure as a value.

Some things exist exactly once: a set of constants, a factory, the entry point of a program. Scala declares them with object, which defines a single instance with no class to instantiate. When an object has the same name as a class and lives in the same file, it is that class's companion, and the two can see each other's private members. The code on the left uses that to guard construction. The constructor of Sku is marked private, so nothing outside can write new Sku with an arbitrary string; that is the commented error. Construction goes through the companion instead. Sku dot parse checks the raw text against a format, three capital letters, a dash, and two digits, and only then builds a Sku. It returns Some of the Sku when the text is valid and None when it is not, so a caller cannot forget that parsing can fail. TEA dash zero one is accepted; lowercase tea space one is not. The guarantee that follows is strong: any Sku anywhere in the program has passed the check. Option is only previewed here. Chapter six covers absence and failure properly.

Most domain data is plain data: an order, a line, a price. Case classes are made for it. Mark a class as a case class, and the compiler adds public fields, construction without new, equality that compares fields, a readable to string, and a method called copy. Copy builds a new value with some fields changed and the rest kept. On the left, b is a copy of a with the id changed to eighteen. The memory card shows what keeping the rest means. Order two is a new object, but its lines and its tags are not new. They are the very same objects that order one points to. Copy copies references. For the list of lines that is perfectly safe, because an immutable list can never change underneath either order. The tags are a mutable array buffer, though, so adding rush through b changes what a sees. Nothing in the code mentioned a. The cure is to keep case class fields immutable, and then sharing stops mattering. One more caution: copy bypasses any validating factory. Making the constructor private makes Scala three hide apply and copy too.

Every domain model is built from two ways of combining types, and naming them makes design choices much clearer. The upper card is a product. An order has an id and a customer and a total, all at once, always. A case class is the natural way to write a product. The lower card is a choice. A status is pending, or paid, or shipped, or cancelled, and it is exactly one of them at a time. Notice where the data lives. Only paid carries a receipt, only shipped carries a tracking number, only cancelled carries a reason. Each piece of data appears only in the case where it means something. Compare that with the common alternative: a status string, plus optional receipt, tracking, and reason fields. That version happily represents a pending order with a tracking number, a state that should be impossible. Enum declares the choice in one place, which makes the set of cases closed. A sealed trait with case classes extending it says the same thing longhand, and appears in older code. Because the set is closed, the compiler knows every case. The next section puts that knowledge to work.

Pattern matching is how code reads a choice type. A match takes a value and tries each case from the top, and the first case whose pattern fits is the one that runs. The method on the left describes a status. Pending is a simple pattern: it matches only the pending case. Paid of r does two things at once. It matches only a paid status, and it binds the receipt inside it to the name r, so the right-hand side can use it. The second case adds a guard, if r is empty. That case fits only when the status is paid and the receipt is empty. Order matters here. Because the guarded case comes first, an empty receipt is caught by it; swap the two, and the general case would take every payment, and the guarded one could never run. Now the important part. Status is closed, so the compiler knows its four cases, and it notices that cancelled is never handled. It warns at compile time. Without that warning, a cancelled order would throw a match error at run time. Be clear about the limit, though: the check proves every case is handled, not that each answer is correct.

Classes often share behaviour without being the same kind of thing. A trait captures that behaviour so classes can mix it in. Priced, on the left, says that anything priced has base cents, which it leaves abstract, and total cents, which defaults to the base. Taxed builds on it. It overrides total cents, calls super to get the default, and adds twenty percent. Then two classes. A one off item is just priced. A subscription is priced and taxed, which Scala three writes with a comma after extends. Now the last two lines. Items is a list of priced values. Its elements have the static type Priced, and that is all the compiler knows about them. Yet when map asks each one for total cents, the one off answers one thousand and the subscription answers twelve hundred. Each element answers as the class it really is. That is dynamic dispatch: the runtime class chooses which method runs, and the static type only promises that some total cents exists. Prefer several small traits combined like this over a deep inheritance chain, where finding out which method actually runs means reading every level.

Two values can be equal without being the same object, and the two questions have different answers. On the left, p one and p two are both prices of five hundred. Double equals on a case class compares fields, so they are equal. Eq asks a different question: are these the very same object in memory? They are not, and the memory card shows the two separate objects. For a plain class that does not define equality, double equals falls back to identity, so two boxes with the same contents compare unequal. Now the dangerous half. Bad is a case class with a var field. One bad value of five hundred goes into a hash set, which files it under the hash of its fields at that moment. Then the program changes its cents to nine hundred. The object is still in the set, but its hash has moved, so asking the set whether it contains b answers false. The element is lost inside the collection. The rule that prevents this is a mutation boundary: fields that take part in equality stay immutable. And remember that a case class by itself enforces no business rules; invariants need a factory or a check.

Scala's collection library is large, and the way to choose from it is to start with the question you will ask. The three order lines on the left are a list, a sequence. A sequence keeps order and keeps duplicates, so the tea appears twice, once per line. Turn the product codes into a set, and the duplicate collapses. A set answers one question very well: is this element present? The next line builds a map. Group map reduce groups the lines by product code, maps each line to its quantity, and then combines the quantities for each code with plus. The result maps tea to three and mug to one. A map answers: what is stored under this key? Asking for a key that is not there, cup zero three, returns None rather than throwing, so absence arrives as a value the caller must handle. The table summarises the choice. One caution belongs with it. A plain set or map makes no promise about iteration order, even when small ones happen to look ordered. When order matters to a report, sort explicitly, or use a sorted map, whose order comes from an ordering you can name and test.

Scala's default collections are immutable. Every operation that seems to change one actually returns a new collection, and the original stays exactly as it was. Mutable collections exist too, and they change in place. The difference becomes visible as soon as two parts of a program hold the same object. In the upper half of the code, shared is a mutable list buffer. Adding five hundred changes that one object, so every name that refers to it, anywhere in the program, now sees three prices. To hand the current contents to someone else safely, the code takes a snapshot with to list, an immutable copy frozen at that moment. The lower half shows the immutable side. Prepending five hundred to owned builds a new list, more, and owned is untouched. Look at the memory card, though. The new list does not copy the old one. It points at it. That is structural sharing, and it is safe for one reason: neither list can ever change. A useful habit follows. Keep mutable buffers local to a single method, return immutable snapshots, and write mutable dot list buffer so the choice is always visible.

Three combinators do most of the work in collection code, and the clearest way to tell them apart is to ask how many outputs a single input can produce. The three orders on the left are labelled one, two, and three, and order two is empty on purpose. Map produces exactly one output for each input. Mapping each order to its number of lines gives two, zero, and one. Three in, three out. Filter produces zero or one. Keeping only orders with lines drops the empty order, and mapping to ids leaves one and three. Flat map produces any number, and flattens them into one list. Each order contributes all of its lines, so the result is the three lines across every order, and mapping to quantities gives two, one, and five. Notice what happened to the empty order: it contributed nothing, and no special case was needed. If you had used map instead of flat map, you would get a list of lists, one inner list per order. Because each step is a pure function of what it receives, a chain of these reads from top to bottom, with the intermediate value visible at every step.

A fold is the general way to turn a collection into a single answer. It walks the collection once, from the left, carrying an accumulator, and at each element it combines the accumulator with that element to make the next accumulator. Whatever is left at the end is the result. A fold needs two things. The first is an initial value. For a sum, that is zero, and look at the second line: zero is also the answer when the list is empty. The initial value is your decision about the empty case, made explicitly. The second is a step function. Here it is underscore plus underscore, so the totals add up to eight thousand nine hundred. Reduce looks similar, but it has no initial value. It starts from the first element, so on an empty list there is nothing to start from, and it throws. Prefer fold left, or reduce option, which returns None. The accumulator does not have to match the element type. The last fold carries a pair, a count and a sum, and computes both in one pass. And remember that sum, max, and group map reduce are folds with names. Use the named one when it fits.

Chapter two used for as a loop. With yield added, it becomes an expression that produces a value, and the compiler treats it as notation for combinators you already know. The upper card asks for every order and every line in that order, keeps the lines with a quantity above one, and yields a label made of the order id and the product code. The lower card is what the compiler writes for you. The outer generator, order taken from orders, becomes a flat map. The last generator, line taken from the order's lines, becomes a map, and the value it produces is whatever the yield says. The guard becomes with filter, which skips the lines that fail the test without building an intermediate list. Run either version, and the result is the same: one colon tea and three colon tea. Order two has no lines, so it contributes nothing, and the mug line fails the guard. This translation is the reason for expressions matter so much. Anything with map and flat map can be written this way, and chapter six uses exactly the same notation to chain operations that might fail. When a for expression confuses you, desugar it by hand.

Every collection so far has been strict: each operation does all of its work immediately. Lazy collections postpone work until an element is actually asked for, and the three kinds on the left differ in what they remember. The iterator is the simplest. Summing it gives forty two fifty, and summing it again gives zero, because reading an iterator consumes it. There is nothing left the second time. A view is a lazy description of a computation. Its map does nothing when the view is defined. The printing happens later, during sum, and it happens again on the second sum, because a view remembers nothing and reruns the whole pipeline on every traversal. The lazy list is the third kind. Each element is computed the first time it is needed, and then kept. That is why it can describe an infinite sequence safely. Taking three computes three, and taking three again reuses them. Two consequences follow. Laziness moves effects in time, so keep printing and mutation out of lazy steps. And a lazy list held by a long-lived name keeps every element it ever computed in memory.

Every collection makes some operations cheap and others expensive, and the table on the left records how the cost of an operation grows as the collection grows. Read it as a model, not a stopwatch. A list is built from linked cells. Taking its head, or prepending a new element, touches one cell, so it is constant. Asking for the element at position i means walking i cells, so it is linear, and appending means walking the whole list. A vector is a wide, shallow tree, and every operation in the table is effectively constant, which makes it a sensible general-purpose default. An array buffer indexes in constant time and appends in amortised constant time, but prepending shifts every element. The code card adds two edges that have nothing to do with speed. Head on an empty list throws, while head option returns None. And sorted gives an order you chose, whereas converting a set to a list gives some order that nobody promised. One pattern to avoid: indexing into a list inside a loop makes the whole loop quadratic. And any claim that one version is faster needs a measurement at realistic sizes.

Some values are simply allowed to be missing. A customer might have a discount code, or might not, and that is not an error. Option puts that fact into the type. An option of string is either Some, holding a string, or None. Because the type says so, every caller has to decide what absence means before it can use the value. The method on the left composes two optional steps. The customer's code is optional. If there is a code, flat map looks it up in the discount table, and that lookup is optional too, because the code might not be in the table. If either step gives None, the None passes straight through to the end, where get or else supplies zero, stated once. Ada's VIP code gives twenty. Bo has no code and gets zero. Cy has a code that is not in the table, and also gets zero. Look at those last two results. They are identical, but the reasons are different, and the option has thrown that difference away. That is exactly right when absence is normal and needs no explanation. When the caller needs to know why something failed, the next section reaches for Either.

Either is the type for an operation that can fail in a way the caller needs to understand. An either of E and A is Right, holding a successful A, or Left, holding a reason of type E. The left side carries the explanation that None could not. The code on the left defines that reason as a domain error model. Import error is an enum, and each case is one kind of failure, carrying the data that describes it. A missing field names the field. A bad number names the field and the raw text that would not parse. Parse quantity turns raw text into a positive integer. Three becomes Right of three. The word three becomes Left of bad number, with the field name and the offending input, which is everything a report needs. Because the error is a closed enum, a caller can match on its cases, and the compiler will check that every kind is handled. Map works on the right side only. Multiplying by the unit price changes a Right, and would pass a Left through untouched. Prefer typed errors to strings: a string can only be read by a person, while an enum can be handled by code.

Not all code reports failure with a value. Plenty of it throws, including Java libraries and the to int method used throughout this course. Try is the adapter between the two styles. It runs a piece of code, and if the code returns, you get Success holding the value; if it throws, you get Failure holding the exception. Forty two parses to Success of forty two. Four x throws a number format exception, and Try catches it as a Failure. The right place for Try is the boundary, wrapped tightly around the call that throws, so you know exactly which step it describes. And it is best converted quickly. Read rate turns the try into an either, and then maps the exception into a message, or better, into your own error type. Be clear about the limits. Try catches only non-fatal exceptions. Fatal ones, like a stack overflow, still escape, as the last line shows, because there is nothing sensible to do with them. Try also cannot help with failures that never throw; a wrong total is still wrong. And wrapping a whole program in one Try hides which step failed.

Reading one line of an order file is a chain of steps, and each step depends on the one before. You cannot read the quantity until you have split the line into fields. A for expression over Either expresses exactly that. Each arrow unwraps a Right and hands its value to the next step. If any step produces a Left, the chain stops, and that Left becomes the result. Look at the steps. Split fields checks that there are three fields. The SKU step uses the companion parser from chapter four, which returns an option, so to right turns its None into an unknown SKU error. Then the quantity, then the price, and only if every step succeeded does yield build the order line. Now trace the bad line in the diagram. Splitting succeeds. The SKU is valid. The quantity is the word two, so parse quantity returns a Left, and the chain stops right there. Parse cents is never evaluated at all, and the result is the quantity error. This is the desugaring from chapter five at work. The for becomes flat map calls, and flat map on Either simply does not call the next step when it holds a Left.

The last section stopped at the first error, and for dependent steps that is the only sensible choice. But not every check depends on another. A quantity and a price can be checked independently, and then stopping early just hides information. The upper card validates a row with a bad quantity and a bad price using the fail-fast for expression. It reports that the quantity is bad and says nothing about the price, because the price was never checked. A person fixing an import file would correct the quantity, resubmit, and only then discover the price problem. One round trip per error. The lower card accumulates instead. Both takes the two independent results. If both are Right, it pairs the values. Otherwise it collects every Left into a list. The same input now reports both problems together. Notice that the error type changed to a list of import errors. The plural is part of the signature, so callers know to expect several. In practice you combine the two styles: accumulate across independent fields, and fail fast within any chain where one step needs the result of another.

A total function gives an answer for every input its type allows. A partial function throws for some of them, and the danger is that its type usually gives no warning. The upper card collects three common partial operations. Get on an option throws when the option is None. Indexing a list with five throws when the list has only two elements. And first, a partial function that matches a non-empty list, throws a match error when given an empty one. Each line type-checks perfectly. The lower card replaces each with a total alternative. Get or else supplies a default instead of assuming Some. Lift, on a list, turns indexing into a function that returns an option, so position five gives None instead of an exception. Lift works on any partial function the same way. And is defined at asks a partial function whether it handles an input before you call it. One misunderstanding is worth heading off. An ordinary function type, A arrow B, is not a promise of totality. Its body can still throw. The type describes what goes in and what comes out when it works. Totality is something you build, with Option, Either, and exhaustive matches.

Chapter five used List of Int and List of String without asking how one list type can hold any element. The answer is a type parameter. Checked, on the left, wraps a value of some type A together with a list of warnings. Its map method takes a function from A to B and produces a checked B, keeping the warnings. Mapping a checked twelve hundred with times two gives a checked Int of twenty four hundred. First or is a generic method: it takes a list of A and a default of the same A, and returns the head or the default. Notice what its body can do with A, which is almost nothing. It cannot add to it or print its length, because the signature promises nothing about A. That restriction is what makes it safe for every type. At each call, the compiler infers A from the arguments. A list of strings with a string default gives A equals String. Now the third call: a list of Ints with a string default. That still compiles, because A widens to a common supertype of both, and the result has lost its useful type. Supplying Int explicitly turns that silent widening into a clear compile error.

A completely unconstrained type parameter is safe, but it also cannot do much. A bound changes that trade. Most expensive, on the left, declares A with an upper bound: A must be a Priced. Inside the method, that bound is what makes underscore dot total cents legal. Every A is guaranteed to be a Priced, and every Priced has total cents. Without the bound, A could be String or Int, and the compiler would reject the call. The bound also works at the call site. Passing a list of strings is refused, because a String is not a Priced. Now the less obvious benefit. The result type is option of A, not option of Priced. Give it a list of gifts, and you get back an option of Gift, still a Gift, with its name available. Compare that with a simpler signature taking a list of Priced. That version would work for the same inputs, but it would return only an option of Priced, and the caller would have lost the knowledge that it was a gift. So the rule of thumb is: use a bound when the result must keep the caller's precise type. When it does not, a plain parameter is simpler to read.

A gift is a priced item. Does it follow that a source of gifts is a source of priced items? Variance is the name for that question, and the answer depends on which direction the values flow. The source trait only produces values; next returns an A. Anything that hands out gifts certainly hands out priced items, so the substitution is safe, and the plus sign declares source covariant. The sink trait only consumes values. A sink that accepts any priced item can certainly accept gifts, so a sink of priced can stand in for a sink of gift. The direction reverses, and the minus sign declares it contravariant. Box both reads and writes its item. Suppose a box of gifts were allowed to be used as a box of priced. Some code could then store an ordinary priced item into it, and code still holding it as a box of gifts would read back something that is not a gift. So box must be invariant, allowing neither substitution. List is covariant, which is why a list of gifts can be passed as a list of priced. That works because List is immutable and declares its parameter with a plus. Immutability alone does not make a type covariant.

There are two ways to leave a type open in a trait, and they express the same contract from different sides. The upper card uses a type parameter. A parser of A promises that parse returns either an import error or an A. The quantity parser extends parser of Int, so the result type appears in its very name. The lower card uses an abstract type member instead. The trait declares a type called Out, without saying what it is, and parse returns either an error or an Out. The quantity parser then fixes Out to be Int inside its own body. Both versions compile, and both describe a parser of integers. The difference is who sees the type, and where. With the parameter, every use names it. A list of parsers of Int is completely clear at a glance. With the member, the type is tucked inside the implementation, which suits types that callers rarely need to mention. It can also make signatures harder to read when the member leaks into other method types. The recommendation for this course is simple. Start with a type parameter, and reach for a type member only when you have a concrete reason.

Order ids and customer ids are both integers, and passing one where the other belongs is a genuine, common bug. The upper card shows why a type alias does not help. Order id and customer id are aliases, second names for Int. The lookup method asks for an order id first, and the call passes them the other way round. It compiles without complaint, because both are simply Int. The lower card defines order id as an opaque type inside an object called Ids. Inside that object, an order id really is an Int, so there is no wrapper and no extra allocation at run time. Outside, it is a completely distinct type. Code there cannot treat an order id as an Int, which is the commented error, and could not pass a customer id in its place. Two decisions are worth keeping apart. One is representation: callers cannot see the Int. The other is validation. Here, from rejects zero and negative numbers and returns an option. An opaque type validates nothing on its own. The guarantee comes from the constructors you choose to provide. Give every id its own opaque type, and the swapped call stops compiling.

Scala three can combine types in two directions. A union, written with a bar, is a value of one type or another. An intersection, written with an ampersand, is a value of both at once. Describe, on the left, takes a key that is an Int or a String. Inside, you cannot use it as either until you find out which, and the match does exactly that. The first case handles the Int side and the second the String side, so together they cover the union, and passing a Double is rejected at the call. For alternatives that are real domain concepts, an enum with named cases is usually clearer. Unions shine for small, local either-or inputs like this one. Label goes the other way. It needs a value that is both priced and named, so it can use the name and the total together. Gift extends both traits, so it qualifies; something with only one of them would not. One warning belongs with matching on types. Type arguments are erased at run time, so a case for a list of Int cannot distinguish it from a list of String. Casts have the same blind spot. They only postpone the failure.

Inference works from context, and nearly every inference failure is a case of too little context, or a type wider than you wanted. The first line on the left defines a lambda with nothing around it. There is no expected type, so the compiler has no way to know what x is, and it says the parameter type is missing. Annotate x as Int, and the function's type follows. The second failure is recursion. Count down calls itself, and to type that inner call the compiler would need the result type it is still in the middle of working out. So recursive methods need their result type written. The third case does compile, and that is the problem. A list mixing an integer and a string infers a wide common supertype. Annotating the val as a list of Int or String keeps the precise union. When you read an error, find the words found and required first. The mismatch is always between those two. Fix one annotation at a time, closest to the error. And notice a design signal. If callers keep needing annotations to use your API, the API is probably too abstract, and a plainer signature would serve them better.

This chapter is about capabilities that the compiler can supply, and it starts with the simplest one: syntax. An extension method adds method-call syntax to a type you did not write. The code on the left extends Int with two methods. Extension, followed by cents of type Int in parentheses, names the receiver, the value that will appear before the dot. Inside are two ordinary definitions. As money formats cents as currency text, with the remainder padded to two digits. With tax adds a percentage. Now the calls read naturally. Four two oh five dot as money gives forty two point zero five. One thousand with tax twenty, then as money, gives twelve point zero zero, and the calls chain from left to right. Int itself has not changed at all. The last line shows what the compiler actually calls: plain functions, with the receiver passed as an argument. That explains the rules. An extension is visible only where it is defined or imported. It cannot add fields, and if the type already has a real method with the same name, the real one wins. Keep a domain's extensions together in one object, so that every import says where they come from.

Some arguments are not data. They are capabilities: how to render a value, how to order two values, how to compare them. Scala lets the compiler pass such arguments for you, and the clearest way to understand that is to start without it. In the upper card, render of A is an ordinary trait with one method, and money render is an ordinary object implementing it for integers. Show takes a value and a render for that value's type, and the call passes money render by hand. There is nothing special here. A capability is just a small dictionary of functions passed as an argument. The lower card changes two things. Given render of Int equals money render marks that value as the default capability for its type. And show now declares its render in a separate list with the keyword using. That tells the compiler it may fill the parameter itself, by finding a given of the right type. So show of four two five zero receives money render without mentioning it. You can still pass it explicitly with using, and it is the same call. And if no matching given exists, the call does not compile. Nothing is guessed at run time.

When a call needs a using parameter, the compiler does not search the whole program. It looks in a small set of places, and knowing them explains almost every error about a missing instance. The first place is the current scope: givens defined right here, or imported here. The second is the companion objects of the types involved. In the code on the left, order's companion defines a given render of order. So show of order seventeen works with no import at all, because the compiler looks in order's companion when it needs a render of order. Rendering a plain Int is different. The only render of Int lives in an object called formats, which is neither in scope nor a companion of Int or Render. So the commented call fails, and the error names exactly the type it could not find. Now the import. Scala three's wildcard import, formats dot star, deliberately does not bring givens in. You must write formats dot given. That makes every import of contextual values visible in the source, so a reader can see where an instance came from. When an instance is the natural default for a type, put it in that type's companion.

The pieces from the last three sections combine into a pattern called a type class. A type class has two parts: a generic trait describing a capability, and instances of that trait for each type that has the capability. Render is one. The interface, render of A, says only that a renderable type can be turned into a string. The companion object holds the instances. Integers render as money. Strings render as themselves. The third instance is the interesting one. It renders a list of any A, provided there is a render of A. It takes that element instance with using, and builds the list instance from it. Watch what happens at the last call. Show of a list of integers asks for a render of list of Int. The compiler finds the list instance, sees that it needs a render of Int, finds that too, and assembles the whole thing at compile time. The result is twelve point zero zero and five point zero five, in brackets. This design is open. A new type gets rendering by adding an instance, without editing the trait or the type. And a type with no instance fails at the call, during compilation, not in production.

Writing using render of A on every generic method gets repetitive, so Scala has a shorthand called a context bound. A colon Render inside the type parameter list means exactly the same as a using parameter of type render of A. Read it as: any A that can be rendered. Show, on the left, declares the bound and then fetches the instance with summon, which retrieves a given by its type. Report is a generic algorithm built on top. It needs to show each item, so it declares the same bound, and the requirement passes along to its callers. Report of a title and two totals produces three lines. You have in fact been using a type class since chapter five. Sorted needs a using ordering of A. Integers have an ordering, so sorting prices simply works. A list of gifts has no ordering, because there is no single obvious way to order gifts, so sorted is rejected at compile time. The simplest fix is usually sort by, with a key that already has an ordering, like the total in cents. Define an ordering of gift itself only when gifts really do have one natural order.

Contextual abstraction removes noise from call sites, and in exchange it hides which value was actually used. This last section is about the cost side of that trade. The code on the left defines two renders for integers, a plain one and a money one, in two objects. Importing both brings two equally good candidates into scope. Neither is more specific than the other, so the compiler refuses to pick and reports them as ambiguous, naming both. That is a good outcome: the problem appears at compile time, with names. Resolve it by passing the one you mean, with using money dot money, or by importing only that one. The final line is the kind of contextual feature to avoid. A given conversion from string to Int would let a string appear wherever an Int is expected, and the compiler would quietly insert a call to to Int. With text like four x, that hidden call throws at run time, and the source shows no call at all. Scala three makes conversions require a feature import, precisely as a warning. Prefer the explicit to int option. Use givens for genuine capabilities, where each type has one sensible instance.

So far, every example has fitted in a single file. The order importer has outgrown that, and this chapter organises it. The first tool is the package. The file on the left declares package orders dot parsing, and imports three domain types from orders dot domain. Packages name things. Visibility decides who may use them, and the parser object shows three levels. Parse line has no modifier, so it is public, the entry point other packages are meant to call. Split fields is marked private in brackets parsing, which makes it visible throughout the parsing package but nowhere else. Tests in the same package can use it, and the report package cannot. Trim all is plain private, a detail of this one object. Now the more important rule, which is about direction. Parsing depends on the domain, so it imports domain types. The domain must never import from parsing. Keeping that one-way arrow means the domain compiles and is tested on its own, with no parsing or input and output code anywhere near it. A good habit follows: start members private, and widen them only when a real caller needs access.

A package only asks for a direction of dependency. Nothing stops a hurried change from importing parsing code into the domain. Build modules turn that request into a rule. The four lines of build dot s b t on the left declare four subprojects, and the graph beneath shows what they make. The domain depends on nothing. It holds the types and rules of an order, with no input or output at all. Parsing depends on the domain, and so does report, but neither depends on the other. The app module sits on top. It holds the main method and wires the other modules together. Each module can use only the modules it depends on. So if someone adds an import of parsing inside the domain, it is no longer a matter for code review. It simply fails to compile. That is the main benefit, and there are others. Each module compiles and tests on its own, which shortens feedback. And sbt will not let you declare a cycle between modules at all. Modules do cost some build complexity, though. Split a project into them when a boundary is worth enforcing, not by default on day one.

A build definition is not just configuration. It is evidence of which compiler, which libraries, and which versions produced a result, so it is worth reading carefully. The first line sets the Scala version for every module in the build. The value on the left is a deliberate placeholder. A real lesson pins an exact patch release and writes it down, and this slide will not pretend to know which release is current when you watch it. The test library version is a placeholder for the same reason. Now the dependency line. The organisation is org dot scalameta, and the library is munit. The double percent sign matters. It appends the Scala binary suffix, so sbt fetches munit underscore three, the build compiled for Scala three. A single percent would take the name literally, which is right for Java libraries that have no suffix. The final percent Test scopes the library to the test classpath, so it never ships inside the application. Source files go under source main scala, tests under source test scala. Before adding any library, check that it actually publishes for your Scala version.

An example-based test is the simplest kind there is. You fix one input, run the code, and state the answer you expect. The suite on the left uses the munit library, and each of its three tests has a different job. The first is the normal path. A valid line, tea zero one, quantity two, at twelve hundred, should give a total of twenty four hundred, wrapped in Right. The second is the failure path. The quantity is the word two, and the test does not merely check that parsing failed. It checks that the failure is exactly a bad number for the field quantity, with the raw text two. Errors are behaviour too, and they deserve the same precision. The third is an edge case. An empty file should total zero. Empty inputs are where loops, folds, and reductions most often go wrong. Notice how the tests are named. Each name states a rule, so when one fails, the report reads like a sentence about what broke. Assert equals compares whole values and shows both sides when they differ. Be honest about what a green suite means: these cases work. It does not show that every case does.

A property-based test states something that should be true for every input, and then checks it against many generated inputs. The upper card states a fact about orders: reversing the order of the lines must not change the total. That is not a restatement of how the total is computed. It is a separate truth about the domain, and code that broke it would be wrong. Look at the generator. Quantities run from one to ninety nine, and prices from one to a hundred thousand. Those ranges are the arithmetic assumptions from chapter two, written down where they can be checked. Widen them carelessly, and the total can overflow Int, and the property starts failing. That is a good thing: it is telling you the assumption matters. The lower card is a property that proves nothing. It compares the total with the sum of quantity times price, which is exactly what the implementation does. If the formula were wrong, both sides would be wrong together, and the test would still pass. And remember what a passing property means: no counterexample was found among the samples tried. When one is found, the library shrinks it to the smallest failing input.

When something fails, two jobs come before any fix. First, make the failure repeatable. Second, read the evidence in the right order. The terminal on the left starts with sbt clean test. Clean throws away every compiled class, so nothing stale from an earlier build can hide or invent an error. The compile error that follows has a code, E zero zero seven, a type mismatch, and an exact position: the report file, line fourteen, column nineteen. Then the two lines that matter most. Found String, required Int. The fix lies between those two types; here, a stray to string at the end. The second half is a run time failure. A number format exception, for the input four x. Notice that the top frames are not your code at all. They belong to Java's integer parsing and to Scala's string operations. Read down until you reach the first frame from your own code: parse quantity, in the line parser, at line twenty one. That is where to start. Finally, write down the command, the input, and the versions that reproduced it. A failure you cannot repeat is a failure you cannot confirm you have fixed.

The order importer has worked on strings typed into the code. This chapter connects it to real files, and reading a file, which looks like a single call, actually involves four decisions. The first is which file. Path dot of builds a path from parts, and a relative path like this one is resolved against the directory the program is started from, which is a common source of file-not-found surprises. The second is whether the file exists and is a regular file. Checking that up front, with the path in the message, turns a confusing failure later into a clear one now. The third is how much to read. Reading a whole file into memory is fine for a known, modest size, so the code checks the size first and refuses anything over five megabytes. That limit is a stated assumption of this importer, not a law of nature. The fourth is the one most often forgotten. A file holds bytes, not text. Text appears only when the bytes are decoded with a character set. Read string with UTF eight names that choice explicitly, and if the bytes are not valid UTF eight, it throws rather than quietly inventing characters.

Everything inside the program has been checked by the compiler. A file has not. It comes from outside, so every row in it is a claim to be verified, not a fact to be trusted. Parse file, on the left, takes the whole text and accounts for every row. It walks the lines with their index, skips blank ones, and runs each remaining row through parse line from chapter six, which returns either an order line or an import error. Then it splits the results in two: the good lines, and the bad ones paired with their line numbers. The sample input has two rows. The first is valid. The second has an x where the quantity belongs, so the result holds one good line, and one error tagged with line two. That line number is what lets a person find and fix the source. Two honesty points. First, the format is documented in the comment: three fields, separated by commas, no quoting. Real CSV allows quoted fields that contain commas, and handling that correctly needs a proper parser, not split. Second, a bad row does not stop the import. The parser reports, and the caller decides what to do about errors.

An open file is a resource. The operating system lends it to your program, and it must be given back, whether the reading succeeded or failed. Using, from scala dot util, takes care of that. Read lines, on the left, opens the file inside using, lends the open source to the body, and closes it on every path out. Several details matter. Because the file is opened inside using, a missing file does not throw. It becomes a failure, as the second call shows. The body calls to list, so every line is read into memory before the source is closed. If reading throws, the file is still closed. And if closing fails as well, that second failure is recorded rather than lost. Now the trap in the last line. Without to list, the body would return get lines, which is a lazy iterator. Using would close the file as soon as the body returns, and the caller would hold an iterator over a closed file, failing on first use. Two more habits. Always read the try that using returns; ignoring it ignores the failure. And recognise APIs like read string that open and close internally. They need no using at all.

Scala compiles to the same bytecode as Java, so the entire Java standard library, and every Java library you can find, is directly callable from Scala. Calling it is the easy part. The real work is at the boundary, because Java reports failure by throwing, and the domain model built in this course expects failures as values. Parse date, on the left, calls local date dot parse, a static method on a Java class, using ordinary Scala syntax. Its documentation says that it throws a date time parse exception when the text is not a valid ISO date. Nothing in the Scala types warns about that; you learn it by reading the Javadoc. So the call is wrapped, and only that exception is caught. That narrowness matters. If some unrelated bug threw a different exception, it should surface, not be relabelled as a bad date. The caught exception is translated once, right here, into a new import error case, bad date, carrying the raw text. Callers now see an either with a domain error, and never need to know a Java exception existed. That is the general pattern: keep each Java call behind a small Scala function whose signature tells the truth.

Java and Scala disagree about two everyday things: how to say a value is absent, and what a collection is. The boundary is where you reconcile them. The upper card reads a property from a Java properties object. When the key is missing, get property returns null. The value is declared as a String, the compiler accepts it, and calling length on it throws a null pointer exception. Scala's String type does not rule out null by default. The lower card guards the boundary. Option applied to a value turns null into None and anything else into Some, so the missing region becomes None, and get or else supplies a default. Wrap every nullable Java return like that, once, where it enters. Collections need a similar decision. The converters turn a Java list into something Scala can use, but as Scala gives you a wrapper over the same Java list, so later changes on the Java side show through. Adding to list makes an immutable copy you own. Scala three also offers an optional explicit nulls mode, which types such returns as String or Null. It helps, but Java can still return null where its own signature never said so.

The entry point is where the program meets whoever runs it, and it has more responsibilities than starting things off. On the left, at main declares import orders with two typed parameters, a path and a maximum number of errors. The generated entry point parses the command line into those types. Run it with ten as a word instead of a number, and it is rejected with a message before any of your code runs. Configuration comes from the environment. The report currency is read once, here, with a stated default of euros. Reading it in one place, at the edge, means nothing deeper in the program depends on the environment, which keeps that code testable. Then the outputs. A successful report goes to standard output. A problem goes to standard error, and the program exits with status one. That exit code is how a shell script, a build, or a scheduler knows the import failed. Printing an error but exiting with zero would report success. One rule about secrets: credentials never belong in code, examples, or log lines. Read them from the environment, and pass only plain values further in.

Put the pieces of this chapter together, and the importer has a clear shape. The diagram shows it as three layers. At the top is the shell that reads the world. It takes the command line arguments, reads the configuration from the environment, and reads the file, safely, with a size limit and a named encoding. Then it hands plain values downward. In the middle is the core, and every function in it is pure. Parse file turns text into good lines and errors. Validation applies the domain rules. Aggregation computes totals per product. Rendering builds the report as a string. None of them opens a file, reads a clock, or looks at the environment. They take values and return values, which is why every one of them can be tested with small, fast examples and no setup at all. At the bottom is the shell that changes the world: the report to standard output, rejected rows to standard error, and the exit code. This separation also tells you where to look when something breaks. Shell bugs are about resources and boundaries; core bugs are about logic. Keep the shell thin, and move any decisions it grows into the core.

The final stage of the importer enriches orders by calling slow external services, and doing that well means doing several things at once. Two words first. Concurrency means several tasks are in progress during the same period. Parallelism means several are running at the very same instant, on different cores. Both share one hazard: mutable state that more than one task can touch. The code on the left starts four threads, and each one adds one to a shared counter a thousand times. You would expect four thousand. You will usually get less, and a different number each time. The memory card shows why. Plus equals one is not a single step. It reads the value, adds one, and writes the result back. Thread one reads fifty seven. Before it writes, thread two also reads fifty seven. Thread one writes fifty eight, then thread two writes fifty eight too, and one increment has vanished. An atomic integer performs the whole update as one indivisible step. Better still, avoid sharing altogether: let each task return its result, and combine the results afterwards. That is exactly what futures make natural.

A future of A is a value that will hold an A, or a failure, at some later time. The important detail is when its work begins. Creating a future, with Future and a block, schedules that block to run immediately. Where does it run? On an execution context, which is a pool of threads. Future takes the execution context as a using parameter, and the given on the second line supplies the global pool. This is chapter eight's contextual mechanism doing real work. Now look at enrich. Calling it with tea zero one returns straight away, before the price has been looked up. The lookup is running on a pool thread while your code carries on. You can compose with the result before it exists. Price dot map times two does not wait. It builds a new future describing a step to run once the price arrives. And if you ask a future for its value early, you get None. Afterwards, you get Some of Success, or Some of Failure. Remember that futures are not lazy. Defining one starts it, whether or not anything ever reads the result. And the global pool is meant for short work that does not block.

Since creating a future starts it, the place where you create one decides what runs at the same time. The two cards on the left combine the same two calls, a price lookup and a stock check, and they differ in exactly one respect. In the upper card, both futures are created inside the for expression. Remember the desugaring: the second generator lives inside a flat map on the first. So check stock is not even created until the price future has completed. The calls run one after the other, and the total time is roughly the price lookup plus the stock check. Sometimes that is exactly right. If the second call needed the price as an input, it would have to wait. But here it does not. In the lower card, both futures are created before the for. By the time the for begins, both calls are already running, and the for only waits for their results. The total time is roughly the slower of the two. So the rule is: when calls are independent, start them early and combine them afterwards. The code shapes look almost identical. The only difference is the point where each future is created.

A future can fail. When the work inside it throws, the future completes holding that exception instead of a value. From there, failure travels through the chain much like a Left travels through an Either. The first line on the left maps over a lookup for a product that does not exist. The lookup fails, so map is skipped entirely, and the result is the same failure. To get back on track, there are two tools. Recover turns chosen failures into a value. Here, a timeout becomes a price of zero. Recover with turns a failure into another future, such as a lookup in a fallback catalogue for an unknown product. Notice that both name specific exception types. A catch-all recover would turn every bug into a silent default price, which is far worse than a visible failure. On complete runs a callback with either a success or a failure, which makes it suitable for logging, but not for program logic, since nothing waits for it. One hazard deserves a name: a future whose result nobody reads can fail without anyone ever seeing the exception. For every call, decide whether a fallback is genuinely correct, or whether the failure belongs in the report.

Enriching an order means looking up a price for every product in it. Those lookups are independent, so they can all run at once, and the question becomes how to combine many futures into one. Future dot sequence does exactly that. It takes a list of futures of Int and turns it inside out, into one future of a list of Int, which completes when all of them have. Traverse does the mapping and the sequencing in one step: give it the SKUs and the lookup function. Two properties of the result are worth stating plainly. First, the results come back in the order of the input, regardless of which lookup happened to finish first. Second, by default, one failure fails the whole thing. If one SKU out of three is unknown, the combined future fails, and the two good prices are lost with it. For an import report, that is usually the wrong outcome. The lower code recovers inside each item instead, turning each lookup into an Either. Now the combined future always succeeds, and it reports a price for every SKU that worked and a reason for every one that did not. Starting thousands of lookups at once is a separate risk, which the next section bounds.

Some work blocks. A legacy client that waits on the network holds its thread for the whole wait, doing nothing useful. A common misunderstanding is that wrapping such a call in a future makes it non-blocking. It does not. It only moves the blocking onto a pool thread. Read legacy, on the left, still occupies one thread for every call in progress. The blocking marker helps a little. It tells the global pool that this thread is about to wait, so the pool can add another thread and keep other work moving. But it cannot make the waiting free. Start ten thousand lookups at once, and you have ten thousand threads waiting. So bound the fan-out, for example by processing the SKUs in batches of eight. Now timeouts. Await result with two seconds stops waiting after two seconds and throws a timeout exception. It does not stop the fetch. The call keeps running, holding its thread and loading the remote service, and its result is simply ignored. In the same way, when a combined future fails, the lookups already started carry on. Ordinary futures have no built-in cancellation. And keep await at the edge of the program, never inside library code.

Every future so far has been completed by the work inside it. A promise lets you complete one yourself. A promise is the write side, and its future is the read side. Hand out p dot future to as many readers as you like, and keep the promise for the code that will produce the answer. The rule is that a promise is completed exactly once. Try success with twelve hundred completes the future and returns true. When a second completion arrives, here a late failure, try failure returns false, because the first completion already won. Two competing sources, a fast cache and a slow service for instance, can race safely this way. The plain success method, by contrast, throws if the promise is already complete, so prefer the try versions whenever completions might race. The lower half is about ownership. A fixed thread pool belongs to the code that created it, and that code must shut it down. Forget, and its threads can keep the program from exiting. Ordinary futures give no structured lifetime: nothing closes resources for you, and nothing cancels work. Effect libraries add exactly those guarantees, and they are a natural next step after this course.

A great deal of the Scala you will meet was written in Scala two. You do not need to write it, but you do need to read it, and the good news is that almost all of it maps onto ideas this course has already covered. The upper card is a Scala two version of the reporting code from chapter eight. The striking thing is one keyword, implicit, doing three different jobs. Implicit val declares a given instance, the default render for integers. Implicit class, extending any val, declares an extension method: as money on an Int. And an implicit parameter list is a using parameter, filled by the compiler from the instances in scope. Scala three gave each job its own keyword, given, extension, and using, which is why the lower card says the same thing more plainly. The other differences are mostly surface: braces throughout, and an underscore where Scala three writes a star in wildcard imports. Read Scala two for its intent, and you will rarely go wrong. Converting a whole codebase is a separate project, though. The compiler can rewrite some syntax, but not every library or macro survives the move unchanged.

Is this library compatible is not one question. It is several, each with its own evidence, and a yes to one of them says nothing about the others. The table on the left lists them. Source compatibility asks whether this code compiles with this compiler. The only reliable evidence is compiling it. Binary compatibility asks whether already compiled classes can be linked together. For Scala libraries, the artifact suffix tells you which compiler built them: underscore three, or underscore two thirteen. Scala three can use many two thirteen artifacts, and the build line with cross version for three use two thirteen asks for exactly that.
