Whether a particular library supports it is something to check, not assume. The JDK question is separate again. Classes compiled for a newer JDK will not load on an older one. Then dependencies. Two of your libraries may require different versions of a third. The build picks one, and sbt evicted shows which version won each conflict. An evicted version can compile cleanly and still fail at run time. And there is maintenance: is anyone still releasing it? Whatever you conclude, record the evidence with the claim: the versions, the command, and the date you checked.

Here is the whole application, with one import traced from the command line to the exit code. Each layer in the diagram is a chapter you have already worked through. The read layer takes typed arguments from at main, reads the currency from the environment with a default, and opens the file with using, in UTF eight, within a size limit. The file has three rows. The pure core parses each row into an either. Row two has the letter x where a quantity belongs, so it becomes a bad number error, carrying its line number: a rejected record. The good rows are aggregated by product with group map reduce, and the report is rendered through the render type class. The enrich layer starts all the price lookups together with traverse, recovering inside each one. The lookup for cup zero three fails, so it is kept as a reason rather than crashing the import: an external failure. Finally, the write layer prints the report for two priced products, writes the two problems to standard error, and exits with status one, meaning done, but not clean. Neither failure was a surprise. Each had a designed place to go, and that is the real outcome of this course.

Sooner or later, someone rewrites clear code to make it faster. The upper card is the clear version from chapter five: group map reduce, one line, obviously correct, returning an immutable map. The lower card is a rewrite for speed. It uses an array, an index, a while loop, and a mutable hash map. Is it faster? Nobody has measured, and that is the point of this section. Start by reasoning. Both versions walk the lines exactly once, so they have the same order of growth. Any difference is a constant factor, and constant factors on the JVM are hard to predict by eye, because the just-in-time compiler optimises running code. What the rewrite certainly costs is visible now: more lines, an index to get wrong, and a mutable map handed to callers, who can change it. Next, reason about allocation, because on the JVM, creating objects is often where the time goes. Then measure, with a benchmarking harness such as JMH, at realistic sizes, after warm-up. Keep the rewrite only if the gain is real and actually needed. In this importer, most of the time is spent reading files and waiting on the network, not in this loop.

Everything in this course was built with Scala's standard library and one small test library. That was deliberate: it kept the ideas visible. Beyond it, the ecosystem offers several directions, and they are genuinely distinct, each with its own concepts and prerequisites. Effect systems, such as Cats Effect and ZIO, add exactly what chapter eleven found missing from futures: cancellation, and resources with a scoped lifetime. Streaming libraries process data larger than memory, with bounded buffers between stages. Service development brings HTTP, JSON, and databases, and with them operational responsibilities like configuration and monitoring. Actor systems such as Pekko model work as messages between supervised actors. Spark has its own companion course. And Scala dot js and Scala Native compile Scala for other platforms, each with its own library support. Choose one of these at a time, and learn its prerequisites before its features. Whichever you choose, keep the habits this course practised. Build small applications and have them reviewed. Investigate failures deliberately. Refine by measurement, not guesswork. And for every new project, check tool and library compatibility again, from evidence.
